title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Cleveland, OH: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Cleveland welders and QC staff: mill, bridge, lake fleet and factory work, Parts A, B and C, online or at your Ohio shop.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Cleveland, Ohio: Six Days to Prepare for the Certified Welding Inspector Exam
html:
Few American cities are as tied to welding as Cleveland. Lincoln Electric, one of the world's biggest makers of welding equipment and consumables, is headquartered in suburban Euclid; a working steel mill still runs in the Flats; and the region's manufacturers, bridge builders and Great Lakes fleets keep thousands of welders busy. That concentration of welding also creates steady demand for people who can inspect it. For Northeast Ohio welders, fitters, QC technicians and engineers who want the AWS Certified Welding Inspector letters after their name, Atlantis NDT offers a six-day (6-day) course built around the AWS exam. AWS runs and grades that exam and grants the certification to those who pass; Atlantis does the teaching beforehand and has no say in the result. To price it for yourself or a crew, send a Cleveland enquiry.

Six days, three exam parts: the short version

The AWS CWI exam has a Fundamentals part (A), a hands-on Practical (B) and an open-book Code Application part (C). The six days map onto those parts: two days of fundamentals, one day rehearsing practical measurement and document work, one day inside your chosen code book, one day of timed mock papers and one day of targeted review with an exam-day checklist. The detailed day plan is on the main CWI exam prep page.

Cleveland candidates take it in one of two ways. Working alone, you get online access to the plan, notes and an Atlantis-written practice bank, with an instructor who replies to your questions in writing. Working for a company that wants several inspectors, you can have the six days run at your plant or shop. There is no open-enrolment class in Cleveland and nothing on a calendar. The course carries no AWS approval or endorsement, and Atlantis never sees, sets or marks AWS exam content.

Northeast Ohio work that needs certified welding inspectors

Steel mill maintenance

Cleveland-Cliffs operates the Cleveland Works steel mill along the Cuyahoga River. Integrated mills run on continuous maintenance welding: hardfacing, crane rail and runway repairs, ladle and vessel shell repairs, conveyor and structural work, often under time pressure during a planned outage. Contractors and in-house maintenance teams need someone who can approve a repair procedure, check that the welder is qualified for it, and accept the finished weld. The defects that worry mill inspectors are cracking in high-carbon and hardened steels and lack of fusion in thick repairs, both of which tie straight back to the metallurgy and discontinuity topics on Part A.

Bridges and highway steel

Cleveland's geography of river valleys means a lot of bridges. The twin George V. Voinovich Bridges carry Interstate 90 across the Cuyahoga valley downtown, and the Ohio Department of Transportation and county engineers maintain hundreds of steel spans across the region. New girders and repair welding are done to AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code, with its own rules for fracture-critical members, and fabricators supplying that work keep certified inspectors on their quality staff. Field repair contractors on bridge rehabilitation jobs need them too.

Lake freighters in the winter layup

Great Lakes shipping stops for the coldest months while the locks close, and many freighters spend that period tied up at lake ports for maintenance. Winter layup means hull plating renewals, hatch coaming repairs and structural welding done on a tight window before the spring sailing date. Inspection on that work follows class and owner requirements, and a CWI is a useful credential for contractors bidding it.

Manufacturing across Cuyahoga and its neighbors

Northeast Ohio makes hydraulics and motion-control components, automotive parts, industrial equipment, valves, pressure vessels and machine bases. Ford's Ohio Assembly Plant sits just west in Avon Lake, and the supplier base that serves auto and truck makers welds brackets, frames and exhaust components at volume. Pressure vessel and boiler shops work to ASME Section IX for procedure and welder qualification. Robotic welding cells are common, and inspecting their output means checking a sample of welds against a drawing and a specification many times a shift.

Energy and pipelines to the east and south

Eastern Ohio's natural gas development brought gathering lines, compressor stations and processing plants, much of it welded to API 1104 or ASME B31 piping codes. Cleveland-area welders and inspectors often travel to that work. Utility gas distribution replacement inside the city adds steady pipe welding as well.

Hospital, university and downtown construction

Cleveland's big healthcare systems and universities rarely stop building, and downtown and lakefront redevelopment adds office, residential and parking structures. Ohio's building code follows the International Building Code model, including its chapter on special inspections, so welding on structural steel frames for larger buildings gets checked by an independent inspection agency on top of the fabricator's own quality control. Agency inspectors on those jobs review welder qualification records, watch joint preparation and preheat, and accept or reject completed field welds. Most of that work is to AWS D1.1, and agencies generally want their welding inspectors to hold the CWI. It is a good fit for candidates who would rather move between sites than stay in one plant.

The AWS Cleveland Section and the city's welding network

Cleveland has its own AWS section, part of District 10. The section holds regular technical meetings and has run joint technical programs with ASM International and the American Ceramic Society at Lincoln Electric's Welding Training & Technology Center. For a candidate, those evenings are a cheap way to meet the welding engineers, inspectors and instructors who make up the local profession. They are also the right place to ask someone senior to confirm your work history for the AWS application, which wants verifiable welding-related experience. Current meeting details are on the section site, reachable through aws.org.

From welding student to inspector: Cleveland programs

Cuyahoga Community College (Tri-C) teaches welding at its Manufacturing Technology Center on Woodland Avenue. Its credentials run from a short Introductory Welding certificate to a one-year Industrial Welding certificate of proficiency and an Industrial Welding associate of applied science. The coursework covers shielded metal arc, gas metal arc, gas tungsten arc and flux cored welding, robotic welding, oxyfuel and plasma cutting, print reading and an introduction to nondestructive testing, and students can test for AWS-standard welder certifications in positions from 2F through 4G. Lincoln Electric also runs a long-established welding school in the area.

That kind of formal training helps at two points on the CWI path. It counts on the education side of the AWS eligibility table, where an associate degree in welding or recognized trade coursework reduces the years of experience you need. And print reading and welding symbol work learned at school give you a head start on Part A.

Where production welders usually lose marks, and how the six days respond

Experienced welders come to the CWI with real skill and some predictable gaps. The course spends its hours on those gaps rather than on welding itself.

  • Symbols read slowly. In the shop you read one drawing many times. On the exam you read dozens of symbols once each, under time. The fundamentals days drill AWS A2.4 symbols until arrow-side and other-side, field welds, contours and dimensions are automatic.
  • Terms used loosely. Shop language and AWS A3.0 terminology differ, and the exam uses the standard terms exactly.
  • Arithmetic. Unit conversions, weld cross-section areas and simple ratios show up on Part A. They are easy marks if practised and expensive if not.
  • Finding things in the code. Part C is open book, but a candidate who has never searched a code under time pressure runs out of clock. Day four is spent locating and applying provisions.
  • Measuring instead of judging. On Part B a fillet that looks right still has to be measured and compared with the documents supplied. The practical day rehearses that habit with real gauges.

Taking the AWS exam as an Ohio candidate

Parts A and C are computer-based tests scheduled at Prometric centers after AWS issues your confirmation letter and eligibility code; AWS puts the number of US centers at more than one hundred, and Cleveland candidates should check Prometric's locator for the closest. Part B is run by AWS at seminar and examination locations on fixed dates, with US applications closing about six weeks before. Published 2026 site codes for Part B sessions include several in Troy, in western Ohio, but the list changes, so confirm current dates and sites on aws.org.

Expect 150 items on Part A. Part B pairs hands-on tasks using AWS-supplied tools and specimens with 46 questions, and Part C's open-book paper runs to about 50 to 65 items. You need 72% or better on every part, and a Prometric session gives you a maximum of two hours on each computer-based paper. Fee schedules for the exam and AWS seminars live on aws.org; to plan the total outlay, see the CWI budget calculator.

Choosing a Part C code in Northeast Ohio

The AWS menu for Part C runs from the steel structural code (D1.1) and its aluminum counterpart (D1.2), through the bridge code (D1.5), the railroad specification (D15.1) and the aerospace specification (D17.1), to API 1104 for pipelines, a combined ASME choice of Section IX with the B31.1 and B31.3 piping codes, and an ISO choice. Mill maintenance, structural fabrication and general manufacturing people usually choose AWS D1.1. Bridge fabricators choose AWS D1.5. Pressure vessel and piping staff tend toward the ASME book, and those heading for gas line work pick API 1104. Exam editions can lag the current printing, so buy the edition AWS names.

Online or at your shop: two ways through the six days

On your own

Self-study suits people on rotating shifts at the mill or in a plant. Work the fundamentals first, keep the code book on your bench at work so it becomes familiar, rehearse measurements on scrap welds, and save the timed papers for the run-up to your Prometric date. Any question that stalls you goes to the instructor in writing.

As a group at your facility

A manufacturer or contractor with several candidates can have the six days delivered at its own site in Northeast Ohio. The practical day then uses production welds and the gauges your inspectors already carry, and the code day runs in the book your work follows. Groups mixing structural and pressure work can split for code practice. Applications remain personal: each person files with AWS, supplies their own vision record and books their own exam.

Experience and vision: what no course can supply

AWS weighs schooling against welding-related experience. A high school diploma calls for five years of qualifying work, a bachelor's in welding engineering or welding technology for one, and less schooling for more. Write down every relevant job now, with dates, the codes you worked to and a person who can confirm it. There is also an eyesight check: AWS wants near-vision and color-perception results recorded on its form by a qualified practitioner, dated inside the period AWS allows before exam day. If you are short on experience, the AWS Certified Associate Welding Inspector is the step below. The CWI requirements guide explains both routes.

Beyond the CWI in Cleveland

AWS keeps a CWI current for nine years, with renewal paperwork at year three and year six. Inspectors in Northeast Ohio build on it in different directions: supplier quality for automotive and industrial customers, Senior CWI for those running inspection programs, or nondestructive testing for those who want to examine below the surface. NDT personnel under ASNT SNT-TC-1A are certified by their employer after method training and documented experience; Atlantis offers SNT-TC-1A-based training, described on NDT training in Cleveland and VT Level 2 training. Local inspection work is described on magnetic particle testing in Cleveland and ultrasonic testing in Cleveland. API in-service inspector certifications are a separate track that API runs, and Atlantis does not train for them.

Other Great Lakes CWI pages, and getting a quote

Neighboring pages cover CWI exam prep in Pittsburgh, Detroit and Cincinnati.

When you ask for a price, tell us the headcount, a short note on each candidate's education and years of welding, the code each plans to sit for Part C, and, for delivery in Northeast Ohio, the site address and the gauges and sample welds available. The Cleveland quote form reaches us directly, and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Does Atlantis run a CWI prep classroom in Cleveland?
faq.a: No. Individuals take the six-day course online with written instructor support; companies with several candidates can have the six days run at their Northeast Ohio plant or shop. Full outline.

faq.q: Who decides whether I pass the CWI exam?
faq.a: AWS. It sets eligibility, runs all three parts, grades them and issues the certification. Atlantis prepares candidates and holds no AWS approval or endorsement.

faq.q: Where can a Cleveland candidate sit Part B?
faq.a: AWS gives the practical at its seminar and exam locations on fixed dates. Published 2026 site codes included sessions in Troy, Ohio, but sites change, so check the AWS schedule. The two computer-based papers are booked separately with Prometric.

faq.q: I weld bridge girders. Which code should I take for Part C?
faq.a: AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code, which AWS lists as a Part C option. See AWS D1.5 for an overview.

faq.q: Does a Tri-C Industrial Welding degree help my eligibility?
faq.a: Usually, yes. AWS lets formal welding schooling stand in for part of the required work history, so a welding associate degree shortens the experience you must document. How your particular Tri-C credential is classed is AWS's call, so confirm it first.

faq.q: What do I need to score on the exam?
faq.a: A 72% minimum applies to every part. Part A is 150 questions; Part B mixes practical tasks with 46 questions; Part C is an open-book paper of about 50 to 65 questions.

faq.q: Can the six days be delivered at our mill or shop?
faq.a: Yes. On-site delivery uses your production welds and gauges, and code practice runs in your book. Send a Cleveland enquiry.

faq.q: Why join the AWS Cleveland Section before the exam?
faq.a: Section evenings seat you next to practising inspectors and welding engineers, some of whom can sign off your work history and most of whom know which local shops are short of inspectors.

faq.q: Are the practice questions copied from AWS exams?
faq.a: No. Atlantis writes every practice item to the published AWS subject areas and has no access to the real exam. Method quizzes are on the NDT practice tests page.

faq.q: Should a Cleveland CWI add NDT training?
faq.a: It widens what you can inspect, especially in mills and pressure shops. Under SNT-TC-1A your employer certifies you after training and experience. See NDT training in Cleveland.
